name: ML engineer situations
description: These situations come up in day-to-day ML engineering work. These situations come up in many workplaces. Pick what you would most likely do in practice, not what the rules say. Every option is something people really do.

questions.question: You sign up for a new model-hosting service that you need for work. Which password do you set?
options: Generate a new one in my password manager, so it is unique.
Make up a new one, so no other account is affected if it leaks.
Adapt one I already use, so I can still remember it.
Reuse one from a private account, so I am set up quickly.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: A teammate must run a job on the GPU cluster tonight, but their account does not have access yet, while yours does. What do you do?
options: Ask whoever grants access for an urgent approval, and wait if it cannot be done tonight.
Do it for them under my account, so my login stays with me.
Log in on their computer and let them work, so they are not blocked.
Send them my login, so they can work on their own tonight.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: An old internal experiment tracker only accepts short passwords. What do you set?
options: A random password at the maximum length, generated by my password manager.
My own mix of letters, numbers and symbols at the maximum length.
A word with a number added, so I can remember it.
A short password I already use elsewhere, so I have one less to remember.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: A teammate emails "check out this notebook" with a link to a website you do not know. What do you do?
options: Ask the sender by phone or chat what it is before opening, since their account could be misused.
Check the link address and open it if it looks legitimate.
Open it, since I know the sender.
Open it and sign in if asked, since I need to see it.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: An unknown sender writes "our benchmark results on your model are here", with a link. What do you do?
options: Check independently who the sender is before doing anything, and report the email if in doubt.
Reply and ask for the details in the email itself, without clicking.
Click to have a look but enter nothing, since it could be genuine.
Click and sign in when asked, since I want to see it.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: An unknown sender emails you an attached file named "collaboration proposal" and asks you to look at it. What do you do?
options: Report it to IT or with the company's report function, without opening it.
Leave it unopened and ask the sender for the details in the email text.
Open it if the email reads professionally, since it is probably genuine.
Open it, since handling such files is part of my job.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You find a pre-trained model checkpoint on a public hub that would save you hours of work. What do you do?
options: Ask IT or security whether I may use it, and wait for the answer.
Check who provides it and what others say about it, then use it.
Use it, and remove it again if it causes problems.
Use it straight away, since the time saving matters most right now.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: Looking for a public dataset, a search leads you to a hosting site you have never heard of. The browser shows a warning. What do you do?
options: Leave the site and look for the dataset elsewhere.
Continue to read, but click nothing despite the warnings.
Continue and browse the site normally, since such warnings are often false alarms and the dataset might be useful.
Download the dataset, since it is what I was looking for.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: A public AI chatbot could quickly explain a stack trace that contains internal code and config. What do you do?
options: Use a tool the company has approved instead.
Replace the internal details with placeholders, then use it.
Remove only the most obvious details, then use it.
Paste it in as it is, since I need the result quickly.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: The developer platform where your profile shows your employer and projects announces that it has changed its privacy defaults. What do you do?
options: Review my settings now, since the change may have exposed more.
Review them the next time I log in.
Read the announcement, and change something only if it clearly affects me.
Ignore the announcement, since my profile only shows ordinary information.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You solved a hard training problem and want to post about it. What do you do?
options: Check what I may share before writing, since details could be confidential.
Post only in general terms, without names or details.
Post it, and take it down if someone objects.
Post it with details and pictures, since concrete stories get attention.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: Someone in an online group asks which models and data your company uses. What do you do?
options: Point to what the company has published, since the rest is not mine to share.
Answer in general terms, to be helpful without specifics.
Share a few details that seem harmless, since the group helps me too.
Answer openly, since most of it could be guessed anyway.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You are working alone in a conference hall and want to step away from your laptop for a few minutes. What do you do?
options: Take the laptop with me, since it holds work data.
Lock it and ask someone nearby to watch it, since I will be back in minutes.
Lock it and leave it, since a locked laptop is protected.
Leave it as it is, since I am only gone for a moment.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You are travelling and must send a sample of a proprietary dataset to a teammate within the hour. Only public Wi-Fi is available. What do you do?
options: Connect through the company VPN or my phone's hotspot, then send it.
Send it over the public Wi-Fi with the company's approved, encrypted tool.
Send it over the public Wi-Fi as a password-protected email attachment, and send the password separately.
Send it over the public Wi-Fi as a normal email attachment, since that is the quickest way.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: On a full train you want to work on evaluation results of an unreleased model. What do you do?
options: Work on it only if nobody can see my screen, otherwise do something else.
Use a privacy filter or turn the screen away, and continue.
Work normally, and switch windows if someone looks.
Work normally, since other passengers are not interested in my screen.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You are about to print a diagram that shows customer data flows. A colleague reminds you to follow the SecureDiag-789 guideline. What do you do?
options: Follow it, as I do every time I print.
Follow the parts of it that I remember.
Ask the colleague what that guideline is, since I do not know it.
Print as usual, since I have never heard of that guideline.

questions.question: You have print-outs of diagrams showing customer data flows that you no longer need. What do you do with them?
options: Shred them or put them in the confidential-waste bin.
Take them home and throw them away there.
Tear them up and put them in the paper recycling.
Put them in the normal paper bin, like any other paper.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You find a USB stick in the meeting room your team uses. What do you do?
options: Hand it to IT without plugging it in, since it could carry malware.
Put it aside without plugging it in.
Plug it into a private device, to see what is on it.
Plug it into my work laptop, to see what is on it.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: Your desk holds print-outs of customer data samples and you leave for lunch. What do you do?
options: Lock them away or take them with me.
Put them in my desk drawer, out of sight.
Turn them face down or cover them.
Leave them as they are, since I will be back soon.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: A teammate calls about a security bug in a production model while you are in a busy café. What do you do?
options: Move somewhere private before talking, or call back later.
Talk, but avoid names and specifics.
Talk quietly, since the matter is urgent.
Talk normally, since nobody here knows the context.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: Someone you do not know is alone in your team's lab area, looking at desks and screens. What do you do?
options: Alert reception or security.
Ask them who they are visiting.
Mention it to a colleague.
Carry on, since visitors are common here.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You notice a teammate regularly pastes API tokens into the team chat. What do you do?
options: Talk to them, and raise it with my lead if it continues.
Mention it to them once and leave it there.
Say nothing to them, but mention it to other colleagues.
Leave it, since how they work is their business.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: Your cloud project account shows a login from a city you have not been to. What do you do?
options: Report it to IT or security right away.
Ask colleagues whether they have seen something similar, and report it if they have.
Watch whether it happens again before doing anything.
Leave it, since nothing seems to have happened.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You realise you shared the results of an evaluation of a new model currently in training with the wrong external person. What do you do?
options: Report it right away and follow the instructions I get on contacting the recipient.
Ask the recipient to delete it, and report it afterwards.
Ask the recipient to delete it, and leave it at that.
Leave it, since the content was not that sensitive.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: The yearly security training, with a new module on AI tools, is due this week, and the sprint is full. What do you do?
options: Do it properly this week, and discuss with my manager which task can wait.
Ask my manager for a short extension, and do it properly then.
Click through it now, since I know most of the content.
Leave it until someone reminds me, since my work comes first.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: Your company announces updated rules for AI coding assistants. What do you do?
options: Read them and change how I work.
Skim them and save the link for when I need it.
Wait for a colleague's summary, since that saves time.
Carry on as before, since my way of working has been fine so far.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: A model release date conflicts with a mandatory security review that allows no exceptions. What would top management most likely decide?
options: The requirement is met, and the deadline moves if needed.
An exception is made only with documented sign-off from security.
The deadline holds, and the requirement is dealt with afterwards.
The deadline holds, and the requirement is dropped.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: A member of top management finds the access process for production data inconvenient for their own work. What most likely happens?
options: They follow it like everyone else, or use an approved alternative.
They follow it most of the time, but skip it when they are under time pressure.
They get an informal exception.
They do it their own way, and nobody objects.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: You want to know whether you may train models on customer data. How easily can you find out what the company's rule is?
options: I already know, since the company has told us clearly.
I know where to look it up.
I would have to ask around.
I am not sure such a rule exists.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: Someone at your company copies a large training dataset to a private device. Would the company notice?
options: Yes, it would be blocked or flagged automatically.
Probably, in a later review.
Only by chance.
No.
Prefer not to answer

questions.question: A rule requires a second person to review every change to the training pipeline, and your small fix must go out today. What do you do?
options: Get the check done first, even if it goes out late.
Get a quick check from whoever is available, and note that it was rushed.
Send it out now and ask for the check afterwards.
Send it out without the check, since it is a small matter.
Prefer not to answer
